title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-275-769-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-275-769-001
Issues
Whether Respondents overcame the Division Independent Medical Examiner’s
⮚
opinion by clear and convincing evidence that Claimant is not at Maximum Medical
Improvement.
Whether the PRP injections recommended by Dr. Sacha are reasonable and
⮚
necessary to treat Claimant from the effects of her work injury.
Whether the treatment recommended by Dr. Reither, the DIME physician, is
⮚
reasonable necessary, and related to treat Claimant from the effects of the work
injury.1
Whether Claimant is entitled to temporary total disability benefits from March 19,
⮚
2025, and continuing, if she is not at MMI.
Stipulations
Respondents stipulated that if Claimant is not at MMI, she is entitled to have TTD
reinstated as of March 19, 2025.
1 Although some testing to complete the DIME can be ordered by an ALJ, the ALJ does not
have the authority to order Respondents to provide treatment which has not been prescribed by
an authorized treating physician. See WCRP 11-2-H; Potter v. Grounds Service Co., W.C. No.
4-935-523-04 (August 15, 2018); Torres v. City and County of Denver, W.C. No. 4-917-329-03
(May 15, 2018). Therefore, this issue will not be addressed.
1

FINDINGS OF FACT
1. Claimant was employed by Employer as a painter.
2. On June 12, 2024, Claimant sustained an admitted industrial injury when she fell from a
ladder while working.
3. After the fall, Claimant was evaluated at the emergency department. Lumbar imaging
showed an acute compression fracture at L1. The initial lumbar CT showed
approximately 10% loss of vertebral body height at L1, with minimal retropulsion and no
evidence of spinal canal narrowing.
4. Claimant was placed in a back brace and referred for follow-up spine evaluation.
5. Claimant subsequently treated through Concentra. Claimant was also referred to Dr.
Michael Rauzzino, a spine surgeon, and underwent physical therapy, was prescribed
medication management, and later underwent pain-management treatment with Dr.
John Sacha.
6. On July 1, 2024, Deana Halat, N.P., documented thoracic tenderness, bilateral muscle
spasms, and limited range of motion. Claimant was released to return to work with
restrictions and referred to Dr. Rauzzino, a surgeon.
7. On July 3, 2024, Dr. Shantell Twobears documented continued low back pain, lumbar
tenderness, and bilateral muscle spasms. Dr. Twobears assessed a lumbar
compression fracture and continued work restrictions.
8. On July 16, 2024, Dr. Rauzzino evaluated Claimant for the L1 compression fracture. He
noted an L1 fracture with approximately 20% loss of height (up from 10%), pain with
lumbar flexion and extension, and recommended Claimant wean from the brace and
begin physical therapy.
9. Claimant underwent an MRI on September 6, 2024, and it showed a superior L1
endplate fracture with 20% loss of height and moderate bone marrow edema,
compatible with a subacute fracture.
2

10.On December 3, 2024, Dr. Rauzzino reevaluated Claimant. Claimant continued to
report severe back pain with activity. Dr. Rauzzino stated that, based on the most recent
imaging, the fracture had not healed despite conservative management. He
recommended an updated lumbar MRI and stated that, if the MRI confirmed the fracture
remained unhealed, he would recommend an L1 kyphoplasty.
11.On December 10, 2024, Claimant returned to Dr. Sacha. On examination, Dr. Sacha
documented lumbar paraspinal spasm from approximately L2 to L5, pain with extension,
extension rotation, and forward flexion, negative straight leg raise, negative bowstring
test, negative neural tension test, and no tenderness over the spinous process of L1-
T12.Dr. Sacha’s impression included L1 compression fracture and secondary lumbar
facet syndrome. He recommended bilateral L2-L5 facet injections under fluoroscopic
guidance and conscious sedation for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. He also
wanted Claimant to follow up after seeing Dr. Rauzzino and after the injections to
assess whether Claimant was at MMI. Claimant agreed to undergo the injections.
12.On December 17, 2024, Claimant had another lumbar MRI. The MRI showed interval
resolution of the previously seen bone marrow edema at L1. The MRI report also
documents a loss of height at L1 of 25% - a 15% increase from the prior MRI - very
minimal kyphosis, and very minimal bony retropulsion. However, the report also
indicates that there were no new findings from the prior MRI. Thus, this report is not
clear as to whether there was an increase in loss of height at L1.
13.On January 7, 2025, Dr. Sacha documented that all further care, including his requested
bilateral L2-L5 facet injections, had been denied pending a respondent’s independent
medical evaluation.
14.On January 28, 2025, Dr. Rauzzino reviewed the December 17, 2024, MRI and opined
that the L1 compression fracture no longer showed edema and was healed. Dr.
Rauzzino recorded that Claimant felt better but continued to have back pain, rated at
4/10 to 5/10. Dr. Rauzzino further recorded that Claimant did not wish to pursue the
injections recommended by Dr. Sacha because the fracture had healed. Dr. Rauzzino
3

opined that Claimant was at MMI from his standpoint, did not require surgery, and
should return to her primary care physician for impairment rating and case closure.
15.On January 30, 2025, Dr. Anant Kumar performed an IME on behalf of Respondents.
Dr. Kumar assessed that Claimant had sustained an L1 compression fracture that had
healed, that the fracture was 100% related to the work injury, that no additional surgical
treatment or physical therapy was required, and that Claimant was at maximum medical
improvement.
16.On March 18, 2025, Dr. Sacha issued a final report placing Claimant at MMI. Dr. Sacha
documented that Claimant had improved somewhat with time, but also noted that
treatment had not been authorized, Claimant had a Division IME scheduled, and
Claimant was proceeding through the legal process. Dr. Sacha stated: “Unfortunately
because treatment has not been authorized, I am going to move forward with case
closure and allow her to go through the legal process.” The ALJ finds this statement
significant because Dr. Sacha had previously recommended bilateral L2-L5 facet
injections for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, and those injections had not been
authorized.
17.On examination, Dr. Sacha continued to document lumbar findings, including lumbar
paraspinal tenderness, pain with forward flexion, extension, and extension rotation,
diminished range of motion primarily with forward flexion, equivocal straight leg raise,
pain localized to the back, intact sensation, and 5/5 motor strength. His impressions
included L1 compression fracture, secondary lumbar facet syndrome, and secondary
lumbar disc.
18.Dr. Sacha assigned work restrictions of no lifting over 30 pounds, bending and twisting
only occasionally, and no stairs or ladders for safety. He assigned a 9% whole person
impairment rating, consisting of 7% whole person impairment for the L1 compression
fracture approaching 30% and 2% whole person impairment for lumbar range of motion.
He found no neurologic impairment and no apportionment.
19.Although Dr. Sacha placed Claimant at MMI, he simultaneously identified additional
treatment he believed should be allowed, including staged bilateral L2-L5 facet
4

injections to a lumbar epidural steroid injection, possible bilateral L2-L5 medial branch
blocks followed by radiofrequency neurotomy, a repeat MRI in six months to assess
changes in the degree of compression fracture, massage therapy, and acupuncture. Dr.
Sacha stated that he was moving forward with MMI and case closure, “but I am putting
on below the recommended care that needs to be done as maintenance.” Based on Dr.
Sacha’s report, the ALJ finds that all further care was denied and that caused Dr. Sacha
to place Claimant at MMI.
20.The ALJ finds that Dr. Sacha’s March 18, 2025, MMI opinion does not persuasively
establish that Claimant had reached MMI. Rather, Dr. Sacha placed Claimant at MMI
after recommended treatment, including the bilateral L2-L5 facet injections, had not
been authorized, while at the same time identifying additional treatment he believed
Claimant should receive that the ALJ finds is curative in nature.
21.The ALJ therefore gives limited weight to Dr. Sacha’s March 18, 2025, MMI opinion on
the issue of whether Claimant was at MMI. The report is more persuasive as evidence
that treatment remained under consideration to cure and relieve Claimant from the
effects of her work injury, rather than evidence that no further treatment was reasonably
expected to improve Claimant’s condition.
22.On April 24, 2025, Respondents filed a Final Admission of Liability based on Dr.
Sacha’s March 18, 2025, report. The Final Admission admitted for the impairment rating
assigned by Dr. Sacha, admitted for maintenance medical treatment, and terminated
TTD as of March 18, 2025.
23.Claimant credibly testified that she has not worked since the June 12, 2024, injury; she
remains unable to perform her pre-injury painting work, which required climbing ladders
and physical activity inconsistent with her restrictions; she continues to have back pain
and that her back pain increases with activity and lifting; she feels swelling or a “ball” in
the painful area of her back. Thus, the ALJ finds Claimant continued to have back pain
and remained unable to perform her regular painting work after March 18, 2025.
5

24.On November 26, 2025, Dr. Braden Reiter performed the Division Independent Medical
Examination. Dr. Reiter reviewed medical records and examined Claimant with the
assistance of a professional interpreter.
25.Dr. Reiter diagnosed an L1 compression fracture with 25% loss of height and lumbar
facet syndrome. On examination, Dr. Reiter found lumbar midline tenderness, lumbar
paraspinal spasm, and increased pain with lumbar extension. Straight leg raise was
negative, sensation was intact, and lower-extremity strength was normal. After his
assessment, Dr. Reiter opined that Claimant was not at maximum medical
improvement.
26.Dr. Reiter concluded Claimant had not reached MMI because she continued to
experience increased back pain limiting her activity and had progression of the L1
compression fracture from approximately 10% loss of height on the initial CT to 25%
loss of height on the December 17, 2024, MRI. Dr. Reiter further relied on the fact that
Claimant obtained temporary improvement from chiropractic care and had been
recommended for further testing and possible further treatment by a spine specialist, as
well as possible injections by physiatry. Dr. Reiter recommended work restrictions of no
lifting, pushing, or pulling greater than 30 pounds, and no crawling, kneeling, squatting,
or climbing ladders.
27.Although Dr. Reiter found Claimant was not at MMI, he assigned a provisional 15%
whole person impairment rating for purposes of the DIME, consisting of 5% whole
person impairment for the L1 compression fracture and 11% whole person impairment
for lumbar range-of-motion impairment.
28.Dr. Reiter recommended additional care consisting of 8 to 10 sessions of chiropractic
treatment, follow-up with Dr. Sacha for evaluation and possible facet injections, follow-
up with a spine specialist for evaluation of the L1 compression fracture, repeat lumbar
MRI, and consideration of possible kyphoplasty. The ALJ finds that Dr. Reiter’s
recommendation for further evaluation and treatment is consistent with his opinion that
Claimant had not reached a stable and stationary condition.
6

29.Dr. Douglas Scott evaluated Claimant for Respondents on February 25, 2026, and
issued a report dated March 11, 2026. Dr. Scott agreed that Claimant sustained an L1
compression fracture as a result of the June 12, 2024, work injury and attributed 100%
of Claimant’s current condition to that injury. However, Dr. Scott disagreed with Dr.
Reiter’s MMI opinion. Dr. Scott diagnosed a healed L1 compression fracture and opined
that Claimant was at MMI as of January 28, 2025, based primarily on Dr. Rauzzino’s
opinion that the L1 fracture had healed. Dr. Scott further opined that no additional
medical or surgical treatment was indicated for the healed L1 compression fracture.
30.Although Dr. Scott found Claimant at MMI, he observed that Claimant appeared
depressed and recommended a psychological evaluation to assess possible
psychological confounders contributing to delayed recovery and chronic pain
complaints. The ALJ does not find that the recommendation for psychological
evaluation, standing alone, proves Claimant was not at MMI. However, the
recommendation qualifies the persuasive weight of Dr. Scott’s MMI opinion because it
shows that even Dr. Scott believed further evaluation was appropriate to assess factors
potentially contributing to Claimant’s ongoing pain complaints.
31.Dr. Scott did not perform two-inclinometer lumbar range-of-motion measurements. He
acknowledged that Dr. Reiter found a valid 11% whole person impairment for lumbar
range-of-motion deficit and did not identify an error in Dr. Reiter’s impairment rating.
32.Dr. Scott assigned work restrictions including no lifting more than 25 pounds from floor
to waist with both hands, avoiding frequent twisting at the waist or deep bending,
avoiding high-impact activities, using upright posture when sitting and standing, and
bending at the hips and knees rather than the back when lifting.
33.Dr. Scott also testified. Dr. Scott testified that Claimant’s L1 compression fracture was
located at the thoracolumbar junction, between T12 and L1. He acknowledged that the
initial L1 height loss was approximately 10%.
34.Dr. Scott acknowledged that the September 6, 2024, MRI showed progression to 20%
height loss and that, structurally, a 20% compression fracture is more pronounced than
a 10% compression fracture. He also acknowledged that the December 17, 2024, MRI
7

showed 25% loss of height at L1. Dr. Scott therefore agreed that the imaging reports
documented progression from approximately 10% to 20% to 25% height loss.
35.Dr. Scott acknowledged that Dr. Reiter relied on the progression from 10% to 25%
height loss as part of his rationale for finding Claimant not at MMI.
36.Dr. Scott also reviewed the March 11, 2026, MRI report, which reported a mild to
moderate chronic L1 compression fracture with 40% loss of vertebral body height. Dr.
Scott testified that the report was internally unclear because it also stated that the
findings were unchanged from the December 17, 2024, MRI. Dr. Scott acknowledged
that, if Claimant’s L1 compression fracture had progressed from 10% to 40% height
loss, that would represent worsening of the compression fracture.
37.Dr. Scott testified that collapse of the vertebral body can alter spinal alignment and
place increased stress on adjacent discs and vertebrae. He also testified that vertebral
collapse can place increased pressure on the facet joints above and below the fracture,
and that additional collapse could provide a basis for Claimant’s continuing back pain.
38.Dr. Scott further testified that, to have a fully stable spine, the vertebral bodies should
be full and not compressed. He acknowledged that progressive compression fractures
may require consideration of medical intervention, including kyphoplasty.
39.Dr. Scott testified that he had no objection to Dr. Reiter’s recommendation for repeat
MRI and spine-specialist review. He understood Dr. Reiter’s recommendation to
consider possible kyphoplasty as a recommendation to send Claimant back to a
surgeon to determine whether kyphoplasty was needed.
40.In his report and testimony, Dr. Scott opined that the facet injections recommended by
Dr. Sacha were not reasonable and necessary. However, Dr. Scott qualified that
opinion at hearing. He testified that, if Claimant had undergone the facet joint injections
recommended or contemplated by Dr. Sacha and discussed by Dr. Reiter, and if
Claimant had a good response, he probably would have reversed his original opinion
and concluded that Claimant had some facet-generated pain. Dr. Scott further testified
8

that Claimant had not undergone those facet injections and that Dr. Sacha was then
requesting PRP injection treatment.
41.The ALJ finds that Dr. Scott’s testimony regarding facet injections does not establish
that Claimant has facet-generated pain. However, it does show that Dr. Scott’s opinion
against facet injections was not absolute and that further diagnostic or injection-based
treatment could have medical significance in determining the extent of Claimant’s work
injury and need for additional curative treatment.
42.The ALJ finds that Dr. Scott’s testimony materially qualifies his report. Although Dr.
Scott continued to opine that Claimant was at MMI, his testimony acknowledged
uncertainty regarding the March 11, 2026, MRI, the potential clinical significance of
progressive vertebral collapse, the potential relationship between vertebral collapse and
adjacent facet pain, the possible need for spine-specialist review and kyphoplasty
evaluation, and the potential diagnostic value of facet injections. The ALJ therefore
gives Dr. Scott’s MMI opinion less weight as to whether Claimant is at MMI.
43.Essentially, Respondents framed the MMI issue around evidence they contend showed
medical stability. Respondents emphasized the December 17, 2024, MRI finding that
the previously seen bone marrow edema had resolved, and relied on the opinions of Dr.
Rauzzino, Dr. Kumar, and Dr. Scott that the L1 compression fracture had healed and
that no further treatment directed to the L1 compression fracture was required.
44.Respondents also emphasized the absence of neurologic findings, the lack of objective
imaging support for facet syndrome or radiculopathy causally related to the L1
compression fracture, and what Respondents contend were inconsistencies in
Claimant’s reported symptoms, functional abilities, desire for injections, and
understanding of whether treatment had been denied.
45.On the other hand, Claimant framed the MMI issue more broadly, relying on the entire
clinical course. Claimant emphasized serial imaging showing progression of L1
vertebral height loss from approximately 10% to 20% to 25%, and possibly 40%,
ongoing back pain and activity limitations, continued work restrictions, Dr. Sacha’s
9

continued treatment recommendations, and Dr. Reiter’s DIME opinion that Claimant had
not reached a stable and stationary condition.
46.The ALJ has considered Respondents’ evidence and arguments, including the
December 17, 2024 MRI finding of resolved bone marrow edema; the opinions of Drs.
Rauzzino, Kumar, and Scott that the L1 compression fracture had healed; the absence
of neurologic findings; and Respondents’ arguments concerning Claimant’s symptom
reporting, functional reporting, the documented inconsistent desire for injections, and
understanding of whether treatment had been denied.
47.The ALJ also considered the opinions of Dr. Rauzzino, Dr. Kumar, and Dr. Scott that
Claimant’s L1 compression fracture had healed and that Claimant had reached MMI.
Those opinions are not ignored. However, Dr. Scott’s testimony materially qualified the
force of Respondents’ evidence.
48.The record contains competing medical interpretations of the December 17, 2024, MRI,
the March 11, 2026, MRI, and Claimant’s ongoing symptoms. Dr. Sacha’s January 7,
2025, note concerning denied care, his March 18, 2025, report, the continuing treatment
recommendations, Claimant’s ongoing symptoms, Dr. Reiter’s explanation concerning
progression of L1 height loss, and Dr. Scott’s hearing testimony support a finding that
Respondents did not prove by clear and convincing evidence that Claimant was at MMI.
49.The ALJ gives significant weight to Dr. Reiter’s DIME opinion because it is consistent
with the documented progression of the L1 compression fracture from approximately
10% height loss to 25% height loss, Claimant’s continuing lumbar symptoms, ongoing
treatment recommendations, Dr. Sacha’s March 18, 2025 statement that case closure
was being pursued because treatment had not been authorized, and Dr. Scott’s
testimony concerning progressive collapse, adjacent facet stress, possible kyphoplasty
evaluation, and diagnostic facet injections.
50.The ALJ finds Claimant’s position and Dr. Reiter’s DIME opinion more persuasive.
Respondents’ arguments do not negate the documented progression of L1 vertebral
height loss from approximately 10% to 25%, Claimant’s continuing lumbar symptoms
10

and restrictions, Dr. Sacha’s continued treatment recommendations, or Dr. Reiter’s
opinion that Claimant was not stable and stationary.
51.The ALJ finds that Respondents established a difference of medical opinion concerning
MMI but did not establish by clear and convincing evidence that Dr. Reiter’s DIME
opinion that Claimant is not at MMI is incorrect.
PRP Injections
57.After the DIME, Dr. Sacha continued to evaluate treatment options for Claimant’s
ongoing lumbar symptoms. On February 13, 2026, Dr. Sacha assessed lumbar
radiculopathy as the primary diagnosis, L1 compression fracture, and opioid use,
complicated. Dr. Sacha discussed a repeat lumbar epidural injection versus an L4-L5
and L5-S1 intradiscal platelet-rich plasma procedure. Claimant elected to proceed with
the intradiscal platelet-rich plasma procedure.
58.Dr. Sacha also noted that, for the L1 compression fracture and symptoms at the
thoracolumbar junction, Claimant was to have an evaluation with Dr. Rauzzino to
determine whether surgery was needed.
59.Dr. Scott disagreed that the PRP procedure was necessary. He stated that the Medical
Treatment Guidelines do not address intradiscal PRP injections and that such injections
can act as a nonsurgical alternative to delay degeneration of the disc.
60.At hearing, Dr. Scott testified that he was not sure PRP was reasonable or necessary,
that PRP was outside the Medical Treatment Guidelines, and that he was not clear what
site Dr. Sacha was advocating for PRP.
61.The ALJ gives Dr. Scott’s disagreement with PRP less weight because it is based in
substantial part on his opinion that Claimant was at MMI and required no additional care
for the healed L1 fracture, an opinion the ALJ does not find sufficient to overcome the
DIME.
62.The ALJ finds that Dr. Sacha’s PRP recommendation is consistent with the DIME
physician’s broader opinion that Claimant was not at MMI and required additional
evaluation and possible injection-based treatment before MMI.
11

63.The ALJ finds that the PRP procedure recommended by Dr. Sacha is reasonable and
necessary to cure or relieve the effects of the industrial injury. In making this finding, the
ALJ credits Dr. Sacha’s treatment recommendation, as supported by Dr. Reiter’s
opinion that Claimant requires further treatment before MMI, over Dr. Scott’s contrary
opinion.
64.The ALJ does not find that Dr. Reiter specifically recommended PRP. Rather, the ALJ
finds that Dr. Reiter recommended further treatment, including follow-up with Dr. Sacha
for possible injections, and that Dr. Sacha later identified PRP as the injection-based
treatment he recommended for Claimant’s ongoing lumbar symptoms. As a result, the
ALJ finds the PRP injections are reasonably necessary to treat Claimant from the
effects of her work injury.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et seq.,
C.R.S. is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical benefits to
injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of litigation.
See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden of proving entitlement to
benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance
of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering all of the evidence,
to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo.
1979). The facts in a workers’ compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither
in favor of the rights of the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a
workers’ compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers' Compensation
proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law judge. University Park
Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637 (Colo. App. 2001). Even if
other evidence in the record may have supported a contrary inference, it is for the ALJ
to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make credibility determinations, and draw plausible
inferences from the evidence. Id. at 641. When determining credibility, the fact finder
12

should consider, among other things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's
testimony and actions; the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or
improbability) of the testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the
testimony has been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Ins. Co. v.
Cline, 57 P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert testimony is a
matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 55 P.3d
186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is subject to conflicting
interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting part or none of the
testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n, 441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be dispositive
of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of evidence or every
inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has rejected evidence contrary
to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals
Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
Whether Claimant is at Maximum Medical Improvement
D. Maximum medical improvement is primarily a medical determination involving diagnosis
of the claimant’s condition. Berg v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 128 P.3d 270 (Colo. App.
2005); Monfort Transportation v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 942 P.2d 1358 (Colo. App.
1997). MMI exists at the point in time when “any medically determinable physical or
mental impairment as a result of injury has become stable and when no further
treatment is reasonably expected to improve the condition.” § 8-40-201(11.5), C.R.S. A
determination of MMI requires the DIME physician to assess, as a matter of diagnosis,
whether the various components of the claimant’s medical condition are causally related
to the industrial injury. Martinez v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 176 P.3d 826 (Colo. App.
2007); Powell v. Aurora Public Schools, W.C. No. 4-974-718-03 (ICAO Mar. 15, 2017).
E. The party seeking to overcome the DIME physician’s finding regarding MMI bears the
burden of proof by clear and convincing evidence. Magnetic Engineering, Inc. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000). Clear and convincing evidence is
13

evidence demonstrating that it is “highly probable” the DIME physician’s opinion is
incorrect. Qual-Med, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 961 P.2d 590, 592 (Colo. App.
1998); Lafont v. WellBridge d/b/a Colorado Athletic Club, W.C. No. 4-914-378-02 (ICAO
June 25, 2015). Stated another way, to overcome a DIME physician’s opinion, there
must be evidence establishing that the DIME physician’s determination is incorrect, and
that evidence must be unmistakable and free from serious or substantial doubt. Adams
v. Sealy, Inc., W.C. No. 4-476-254 (ICAO Oct. 4, 2001). A mere difference of medical
opinion does not constitute clear and convincing evidence sufficient to overcome the
opinion of the DIME physician. Javalera v. Monte Vista Head Start, Inc., W.C. Nos. 4-
532-166 & 4-523-097 (ICAO July 19, 2004). When a DIME physician issues conflicting
or ambiguous opinions concerning MMI, the ALJ may resolve the inconsistency as a
matter of fact to determine the DIME physician’s true opinion. MGM Supply Co. v.
Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 62 P.3d 1001 (Colo. App. 2002); Licata v. Wholly Cannoli
Café, W.C. No. 4-863-323-04 (ICAO July 26, 2016).
F. Respondents relied on evidence they contend showed that Claimant’s L1 compression
fracture had healed and stabilized. Respondents emphasized the December 17, 2024
MRI finding that the previously seen bone marrow edema had resolved, the opinions of
Dr. Rauzzino, Dr. Kumar, and Dr. Scott that the L1 compression fracture had healed,
the absence of neurologic findings, and the alleged lack of objective imaging support for
facet syndrome or radiculopathy causally related to the L1 fracture. Respondents also
emphasized what they contend were inconsistencies in Claimant’s reported symptoms,
functional abilities, desire for injections, and understanding of whether treatment had
been denied.
G. Claimant relied on the full course of the medical evidence, including serial imaging
showing progression of L1 height loss from approximately 10% on the initial CT to 20%
on the September 6, 2024 MRI and 25% on the December 17, 2024 MRI, ongoing back
pain and activity limitations, continued work restrictions, objective examination findings
including lumbar spasm and pain with extension, Dr. Sacha’s continued treatment
14

recommendations, and Dr. Reiter’s DIME opinion that Claimant had not reached a
stable and stationary condition.
H. The ALJ finds Claimant’s evidence and Dr. Reiter’s DIME opinion more persuasive. The
existence of imaging evidence that may support a finding of fracture healing does not,
by itself, establish MMI where the record also reflects continued symptoms, restrictions,
and treatment recommendations. MMI requires more than evidence that one imaging
feature has improved or resolved; it requires proof that the injury-related condition has
become stable and that no further treatment is reasonably expected to improve the
condition.
I. The ALJ is not persuaded that resolution of bone marrow edema on the December 17,
2024, MRI establishes MMI by clear and convincing evidence. The same MRI showed
25% height loss at L1, and the record continued to reflect lumbar symptoms, work
restrictions, and additional treatment recommendations.
J. The ALJ is also not persuaded that Dr. Sacha’s March 18, 2025, MMI opinion supports
a finding that Claimant was at MMI when he placed her at MMI. Dr. Sacha expressly
stated that he was moving forward with case closure and placing Claimant at MMI
because additional treatment had not been authorized and Claimant would proceed
through the legal process. He also recommended additional treatment, including
injections, possible medial branch blocks and radiofrequency neurotomy, repeat MRI,
massage therapy, and acupuncture. His report therefore does not establish that
Claimant was at MMI.
K. Dr. Scott’s opinion does not overcome the DIME. Although Dr. Scott opined that the
fracture was healed and Claimant was at MMI, he agreed that Claimant sustained the
L1 compression fracture in the industrial injury, apportioned 100% of Claimant’s current
condition to the work injury, assigned ongoing restrictions, and identified no error in Dr.
Reiter’s impairment rating. At hearing, Dr. Scott also acknowledged that the L1
compression fracture progressed from 10% to 25% height loss, that additional collapse
could explain continuing back pain, that progressive compression fractures may require
consideration of kyphoplasty, and that a positive response to facet injections could
15

cause him to reverse his opinion regarding facet-generated pain. His opinion is
therefore insufficient to satisfy Respondents’ clear-and-convincing burden.
L. The totality of the evidence relied upon by Respondents creates a mere difference in
medical opinion between medical providers, but it does not satisfy the clear-and-
convincing standard. Respondents did not prove that Dr. Reiter’s not-at-MMI opinion
was highly probable to be incorrect or free from serious or substantial doubt.
M. As a result, the ALJ finds and concludes Respondents failed to overcome Dr. Reiter’s
DIME opinion Claimant that Claimant is not at MMI by clear and convincing evidence.
Whether the PRP injections are reasonable and necessary
to cure and relieve Claimant from the effects of the industrial injury
N. Respondents are liable to provide medical treatment that is reasonable and necessary
to cure and relieve the effects of the industrial injury. § 8-42-101(1)(a), C.R.S. The
question of whether Claimant proved that treatment is reasonable and necessary is one
of fact for the ALJ. Kroupa v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 53 P.3d 1192 (Colo. App.
2002).
O. When determining whether proposed medical treatment is reasonable and necessary,
the ALJ may consider the provisions and treatment protocols of the Medical Treatment
Guidelines because they represent accepted standards of practice in workers’
compensation cases and were adopted pursuant to an express grant of statutory
authority. However, evidence of compliance or non-compliance with the Medical
Treatment Guidelines is not dispositive of whether medical treatment is reasonable and
necessary. Rather, the ALJ may give evidence regarding compliance with the Medical
Treatment Guidelines such weight as the ALJ determines it is entitled to after
considering the totality of the evidence. Adame v. SSC Berthoud Operating Co., LLC,
W.C. No. 4-784-709 (ICAO Jan. 25, 2012); Thomas v. Four Corners Health Care, W.C.
No. 4-484-220 (ICAO Apr. 27, 2009); Stamey v. C2 Utility Contractors, Inc., W.C. No. 4-
503-974 (ICAO Aug. 21, 2008); see also § 8-43-201(3), C.R.S.
16

P. Dr. Reiter determined that Claimant was not at MMI and required further medical
evaluation and treatment before she could be considered stable and stationary. Dr.
Reiter recommended follow-up with Dr. Sacha for evaluation and possible injections,
follow-up with a spine specialist for evaluation of the L1 compression fracture, repeat
lumbar MRI, and consideration of possible kyphoplasty. The ALJ does not order those
treatments merely because Dr. Reiter identified them in the DIME report. Rather, the
ALJ considers Dr. Reiter’s opinion as persuasive evidence that Claimant remained
symptomatic, was not stable and stationary, and required additional treatment before
MMI.
Q. The specific treatment at issue is the PRP injections recommended by Dr. Sacha, an
authorized treating physician. Dr. Sacha documented persistent lumbar symptoms,
lumbar paraspinal spasm, pain with forward flexion and extension, and ongoing
functional limitations. Dr. Sacha initially recommended interventional treatment in the
form of facet injections and later recommended an intradiscal platelet-rich plasma
procedure for Claimant’s ongoing lumbar symptoms. The ALJ credits Dr. Sacha’s
recommendation because it is consistent with the broader medical picture accepted by
the DIME physician: Claimant was not at MMI, continued to have activity-limiting lumbar
symptoms, and required further evaluation and injection-based treatment.
R. The ALJ recognizes that Dr. Scott disagreed with the need for additional treatment,
including PRP injections. The ALJ gives Dr. Scott’s opinion less weight on this issue
because it depends substantially on his opinion that Claimant’s L1 compression fracture
had healed and that Claimant was at MMI, an opinion the ALJ has rejected as
insufficient to overcome the DIME. Dr. Scott also testified that he was not clear what site
Dr. Sacha was advocating for PRP and that his objection was based in part on the
absence of PRP from the Medical Treatment Guidelines. Considering the totality of the
evidence, Dr. Scott’s testimony establishes a contrary medical opinion that the ALJ
does not find persuasive. Thus, it does not persuade the ALJ that the PRP procedure
recommended by Dr. Sacha is unreasonable, unnecessary, or unrelated.
17

S. The ALJ does not find the Medical Treatment Guidelines dispositive of the PRP issue.
To the extent Respondents rely on the absence of a specific PRP recommendation or
protocol in the Medical Treatment Guidelines, the ALJ gives that evidence limited
weight. The Guidelines may be considered, but they do not control the factual
determination of whether treatment is reasonable and necessary. Here, the totality of
the persuasive evidence supports authorization of the PRP injections: Dr. Sacha is the
authorized treating physician recommending the procedure; Claimant has persistent
lumbar symptoms and functional limitations; Dr. Sacha recommended injection-based
care; Dr. Reiter’s DIME opinion supports the need for further treatment before MMI; and
Dr. Scott’s contrary testimony was qualified and did not persuade the ALJ that the
treatment is unreasonable, unnecessary, or unrelated.
T. As a result, the ALJ finds and concludes that Claimant proved by a preponderance of
the evidence that the PRP injections recommended by Dr. Sacha are reasonable,
necessary, and causally related medical treatment to cure and relieve Claimant from the
effects of the industrial injury.
Whether the treatment recommended by Dr. Reither, the DIME physician, is
reasonable necessary to treat Claimant from the effects of the work injury.
U. Although some testing to complete the DIME can be ordered by an ALJ, the ALJ does
not have the authority to order Respondents to provide treatment which has not been
prescribed by an authorized treating physician. See WCRP 11-2-H; Potter v. Grounds
Service Co., W.C. No. 4-935-523-04 (August 15, 2018); Torres v. City and County of
Denver, W.C. No. 4-917-329-03 (May 15, 2018).
V. Because the ALJ does not have jurisdiction to award treatment suggested by the DIME
physician, such treatment recommendations will not be considered in this order.
Whether Claimant is entitled to temporary total disability
benefits from March 19, 2025, and continuing, if she is not at MMI.
W. Respondents stipulated that TTD would be payable from March 19, 2025, forward, if
Claimant is not at MMI. Since the ALJ has found that Respondents have failed to
18

overcome the DIME opinion that Claimant is not at MMI, Claimant is entitled to have her
TTD reinstated as of March 19, 2025.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant is not at MMI and is entitled to reasonable and necessary medical
treatment to cure and relieve her from the effects of her work injury.
2. Respondents shall pay for the PRP injections recommended by Dr. Sacha.
3. Respondents shall reinstate Claimant’s TTD benefits as of March 19, 2025, and
TTD benefits shall be payable until terminated by law.
4. Respondents may take a credit for any PPD paid against TTD that is payable.
5. The ALJ is without jurisdiction to consider whether the treatment recommended
by Dr. Reiter, the DIME physician, is reasonable and necessary to treat Claimant
from the effects of her work injury.
6. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
